Name: narrative_order_bottleneck
Title: Thinking in Reading Order: Does Natural Language's Linear Narrative Constraint Bottleneck LLM Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Because natural language forces information into a single linear sequence, LLMs tend to reason in the surface (narrative) order that premises are presented rather than in the logical dependency order a problem requires, and the mismatch between narrative order and logical-dependency order causally degrades reasoning. We hypothesize that (a) this narrative-order mismatch predicts per-problem failure, (b) forcing the model to explicitly reconstruct the dependency order before reasoning causally recovers most of the lost accuracy, and (c) a training-free attention diagnostic reveals over-reliance on locally-recent (narrative-adjacent) premises.
Related Work: Liu et al. (2025, Language-of-Thoughts) show LLMs inherit 'language modeling biases' that focus reasoning on a biased part of the premise and propose LoT prompting to reorder expressions; several works (Feng et al. 2024 POI; Guo et al. 2025 herbarium) note candidate-order sensitivity. Prior work on premise-order effects (e.g., Chen et al. on premise ordering in reasoning) shows shuffling premises hurts accuracy. These works document order sensitivity or offer a single prompting fix, but none (1) formalize a per-problem quantitative mismatch between the presented narrative order and the problem's true logical-dependency DAG, (2) test whether that mismatch metric predicts failure, (3) provide an attention-based mechanistic diagnostic linking failure to recency-biased premise reliance, or (4) causally compare a dependency-reconstruction intervention against surface reordering to isolate whether the bottleneck is the linear-order constraint itself versus mere token adjacency. We contribute a graded, controllable narrative-order manipulation with a ground-truth dependency structure, turning a documented curiosity into a measurable, predictable, and repairable property of language-based reasoning.
Abstract: Natural language is intrinsically linear: it forces the premises of a problem into a single reading order, even when the logic connecting them forms a non-linear dependency structure. We ask whether this linear-narrative constraint is a genuine bottleneck on LLM reasoning. We construct reasoning problems (multi-step arithmetic word problems, multi-hop factual chains, and constraint-satisfaction/logic puzzles) with an explicit ground-truth logical-dependency DAG, then render each problem under controlled narrative orders ranging from fully dependency-aligned to maximally scrambled, holding content fixed. Using open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2), we define a per-problem Order-Mismatch score (edit/inversion distance between presented order and a topological order of the dependency DAG) and test whether it predicts final-answer failure via mixed-effects logistic regression, controlling for length and difficulty. We then run causal interventions: (i) surface reordering (physically reorder premises into dependency order) and (ii) Dependency-Reconstruction prompting, where the model must first restate the premises in inferred logical order before reasoning, and compare which better recovers accuracy. Mechanistically, we measure whether attention to premises is biased toward narrative-recent tokens rather than logically-relevant ones, and whether this recency bias mediates errors. We predict Order-Mismatch strongly predicts failure, dependency reconstruction recovers most of the gap even without physical reordering, and attention recency bias mediates the effect. Results would reframe a robustness quirk as a fundamental consequence of language's linearity on machine reasoning, informing prompt design, benchmark construction, and theories of language–thought coupling in AI.
Experiments: 1) DATASET WITH DEPENDENCY GROUND TRUTH: Build/adapt ~400 problems across 3 families where each problem has an explicit logical-dependency DAG: (a) multi-step arithmetic word problems where each computation depends on specified prior quantities, (b) 2–4-hop factual chains with named bridge entities, (c) constraint-satisfaction/logic puzzles (e.g., ordering/assignment) with a clause dependency graph. For each, annotate the DAG programmatically from the generator. 2) CONTROLLED NARRATIVE ORDERS: For each problem, generate multiple renderings that vary only premise order—dependency-aligned (topological), reverse-topological, and k levels of random scramble—holding wording and content fixed; verify semantic equivalence automatically. Compute per-rendering Order-Mismatch = normalized inversion/edit distance from a valid topological order of the DAG. 3) MAIN EFFECT + PREDICTION: Run each rendering on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B; record final-answer accuracy. Fit mixed-effects logistic regression: correct ~ Order-Mismatch + log(#tokens) + difficulty + (1|problem) + (1|model); report coefficient, effect size, and per-model AUC of Order-Mismatch as a failure predictor. 4) CAUSAL INTERVENTIONS: (i) SURFACE REORDER—physically reorder premises into topological order and re-run; (ii) DEPENDENCY-RECONSTRUCTION prompt—instruct the model to first list all premises in inferred logical/dependency order, then solve, WITHOUT physically reordering the input; (iii) control prompt that asks to 'restate premises' in original order (to control for the extra restating step). Compare accuracy recovery across interventions; the key test is whether reconstruction (i.e., letting the model re-linearize internally) matches physical reordering, isolating the linearity constraint from token adjacency. 5) MECHANISTIC MEDIATION: For a subset, extract attention from later reasoning tokens back to premise tokens; compute a Recency-Bias score = attention mass on narrative-recent premises minus attention on logically-relevant (DAG-parent) premises. Test whether Recency-Bias correlates with Order-Mismatch and mediates failure (mediation analysis: Order-Mismatch → Recency-Bias → error). 6) GENERALIZATION: test whether the intervention that helps most transfers across the 3 task families and across model sizes; report interaction with DAG width/depth (predict larger mismatch effects for wider, less-linear DAGs). METRICS: accuracy, Order-Mismatch regression coefficient and AUC, per-intervention accuracy recovery (% of gap closed), Recency-Bias correlation and mediation effect, DAG-shape interaction coefficients; all with effect sizes and CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Defining a clean logical-dependency DAG is only tractable for structured problems; naturalistic reasoning may lack a unique DAG—mitigated by using generators with known structure and reporting task-family differences. 2) A DAG may admit multiple valid topological orders, complicating Order-Mismatch; we use minimum distance to the set of valid orders. 3) Dependency-Reconstruction prompting adds tokens/serial compute, confounding with mere extra computation—addressed by the 'restate-in-original-order' control and token-count covariates. 4) Attention is an imperfect mechanistic signal; we corroborate with the behavioral mediation and treat attention analysis as supporting, not definitive. 5) Effects may be model- or scale-specific; we test multiple families/sizes and report scaling. 6) Content-fixed reorderings may still subtly change fluency; automated equivalence checks and human spot-checks mitigate this. 7) If reordering does not help, that itself is informative about whether linearity is the bottleneck versus deeper structural limits.
